quotes.text: كفى بالمرء جهلا ان لا يعرف قدره
كونوا دعاه الى الله به غير السنتكم

connections.label: Self-control begins with directing natural desires rather than suppressing them
Self-building and fulfilling one's duty
Sincere action and the responsibility of influence

chunks.title: The teacher's role is an extension of teaching and prophetic formation
chunks.text: Mazaheri frames teaching as a morally elevated vocation: the teacher participates in the work of divine and prophetic education. The Qur'anic emphasis on teaching is presented together with purification and formation, so education is not merely transferring information.

chunks.title: Guiding one person can be greater than worldly gain
chunks.text: The lesson of the Khaybar narration is that guiding a person toward the straight path carries extraordinary value. Mazaheri uses it to shift the teacher's measure of success from ordinary worldly achievement to transforming a human life.

chunks.title: Education can counter inherited and environmental influences
chunks.text: The chapter identifies four powerful formative influences: heredity, family upbringing, environment, and nourishment. The teacher's influence can counteract these forces, so education is presented as a genuine intervention in a person's formation rather than a passive reflection of circumstances.

chunks.title: A teacher can become a turning point in a person's moral development
chunks.text: The stories of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and the son of Yazid are used to show how a teacher's influence can become the decisive spark that changes a person's moral direction even when family, environment, and upbringing point elsewhere.

chunks.title: Great influence creates great responsibility
chunks.text: Because a teacher can build or damage a student's beliefs and character, teaching carries a correspondingly heavy moral responsibility. Mazaheri warns that harmful instruction can have consequences comparable to causing a person's spiritual destruction.

chunks.title: Example is more powerful than speech alone
chunks.text: The advice to call people toward God through conduct as well as speech establishes a practical principle of education: students absorb the teacher's behavior, not merely the teacher's explicit lessons.

chunks.title: Self-building precedes building others
chunks.text: The chapter applies the principle of self-construction to teachers and other people with influence over others. A person who has not worked on himself cannot reliably produce the same formation in someone else.

chunks.title: Intellectual humility is part of responsible teaching
chunks.text: Mazaheri insists that a teacher must distinguish knowledge from ignorance. Saying 'I do not know' is presented as a form of intellectual honesty that prevents an uninformed answer from becoming a false foundation in a student's mind.

chunks.title: Duty must be fulfilled carefully because entrusted time is not recoverable
chunks.text: The chapter closes by connecting educational responsibility with faithful performance of duty. Teachers should use their opportunity well, prepare for class, think before speaking, and recognize that the trust placed in them includes both teaching and moral formation.

units.title: گفتار دوم : گناه و تعديل غرايز

quotes.text: من حاول أمراً بمعصية الله فهو أفوت لما يرجوا و أسرع لما يحذر
عليك بصدق الحديث و أداء الامانه

connections.label: Moral formation and responsibility for how desires are directed
The inner struggle between desire and spiritual agency
Duty, self-discipline and lawful fulfillment of life
Sincere action versus self-serving motives

chunks.title: The governing rule: a goal pursued through sin turns against the seeker
chunks.text: Mazaheri builds the chapter around Imam al-Husayn's maxim that a person who tries to obtain something through disobedience to God will lose what he seeks and move rapidly toward what he fears. The principle is presented as a practical law of life, not merely an abstract moral warning.

chunks.title: Islam does not require destroying natural desires
chunks.text: Human beings possess natural drives and inclinations, and Mazaheri argues that Islam does not command their elimination. The Qur'anic balance is to seek the hereafter without forgetting one's lawful share of worldly life.

chunks.title: The problem is not desire but the way desire is satisfied
chunks.text: Natural drives such as wealth, status, family provision and social standing can be fulfilled through lawful effort or through sin. The same desire may therefore lead either toward constructive development or toward moral collapse depending on the method used to satisfy it.

chunks.title: Umar ibn Sa'd illustrates desire overpowering moral judgment
chunks.text: Umar ibn Sa'd's decision before Karbala is presented as an example of the conflict between spiritual judgment and animal desire. His attraction to political authority and material benefit gradually overcomes his moral hesitation, after which he rationalizes the decision by promising himself future repentance.

chunks.title: Sin can produce the opposite of the worldly benefit it promises
chunks.text: The later humiliation of Umar ibn Sa'd is used as the concrete fulfillment of Imam al-Husayn's maxim: the attempt to obtain worldly authority through wrongdoing not only destroys the person's moral future but also brings humiliation and loss in the very worldly sphere he sought to secure.

chunks.title: Righteousness protects one's descendants better than sinful accumulation
chunks.text: The story of Moses and al-Khidr's wall is interpreted as evidence that a parent's righteousness can become protection for vulnerable descendants. Mazaheri contrasts this with the attempt to secure children materially through lies, slander, injustice or unlawful wealth.

chunks.title: A good life is linked to righteous action and faith
chunks.text: The chapter connects a wholesome worldly life and the afterlife reward to righteous action joined with faith. Wealth, comfort and apparent success are not treated as reliable measures of a good life when the person's relationship with God is broken.

chunks.title: Trust and honest work are part of lawful desire-management
chunks.text: The story of Abd al-Rahman ibn Sababah illustrates the practical virtues of truthful dealing and returning entrusted property. Mazaheri applies the principle to teachers: accepting money while failing to deliver the entrusted work becomes a form of cheating and moral betrayal.

chunks.title: Preparation and faithful performance are moral obligations
chunks.text: The chapter extends the warning against cheating to professional responsibility. A person who accepts compensation but deliberately underperforms has taken more than he gives, making the Qur'anic warning against fraud relevant to ordinary work as well as commerce.

units.title: گفتار سوم : جهاد با نفس
quotes: إنسان مركب از « روح و جسم »

connections.label: Lawful regulation of natural desires becomes disciplined self-mastery
Jihad with the self develops through concrete virtues and resistance to desire
Sincerity and spiritual agency depend on directing the self rather than serving it

chunks.title: Human beings are uniquely capable of moral and spiritual development
chunks.text: Mazaheri describes the human being as having both an animal/material dimension and a spiritual/kingdom-like dimension. The tension between them creates the possibility of deliberate ascent rather than fixed instinctive behavior.

chunks.title: The animal dimension is a vehicle, not an enemy to be destroyed
chunks.text: The body's desires are not presented as something to annihilate. The task of jihad with the self is to regulate them so that bodily life becomes a means for spiritual movement.

chunks.title: Spiritual pleasures and bodily pleasures can pull in opposite directions
chunks.text: Truth-seeking, knowledge, sacrifice and self-restraint may be difficult for the bodily dimension while food, rest and sexual gratification satisfy it. Moral growth therefore requires learning to choose the higher good when the two directions conflict.

chunks.title: Self-control is the mechanism of spiritual ascent
chunks.text: The recurring metaphor is riding and training a difficult mount: when a person controls desires rather than being controlled by them, the same human faculties become instruments of ascent.

chunks.title: The chapter connects extraordinary spiritual capacities with disciplined self-control
chunks.text: Stories of Jaber al-Ju'fi and Asif ibn Barkhiya are presented as examples of capacities that Mazaheri connects to mastery of the self and Qur'anic knowledge. The practical lesson is not to chase miracles, but to understand the claimed relationship between spiritual discipline and human potential.

chunks.title: The Qur'an is presented as a source of human knowledge and formation
chunks.text: The chapter repeatedly returns to Qur'anic evidence and argues that people who seek clarity, knowledge and spiritual development should maintain an active relationship with the Qur'an.

chunks.title: The human being accepted a responsibility that other created beings did not carry
chunks.text: The discussion of the trust (amanah) in Qur'an 33:72 is used to emphasize both human potential and human liability: the same human being who can rise very high can also be profoundly unjust and ignorant toward himself.

chunks.title: Knowing what a human being is is foundational to ethics and education
chunks.text: Mazaheri criticizes one-dimensional pictures of the human person. If a person is reduced to bodily or social needs alone, moral education cannot explain the full range of human aspiration.

chunks.title: The practical beginning of jihad with the self is mastery rather than suppression
chunks.text: The chapter ultimately makes the central practical point: a person should not surrender to appetite, anger and other impulses, nor imagine that holiness requires becoming less human. The work is to place the animal dimension under rational and spiritual direction.

chunks.title: The chapter develops the practical discipline of jihad with the self
chunks.text: This unit continues the book's central movement from understanding the two dimensions of the human being toward the practical work required to govern the lower self.

chunks.title: Self-mastery is gradual rather than instantaneous
chunks.text: The struggle with the self is presented as repeated training: the person strengthens will through practice, resistance and returning to the right course after failure.

chunks.title: The goal is transformation of the whole person
chunks.text: Jihad is not a narrow battle against one desire. It aims at a reordered person whose intellect, conscience, desires and conduct increasingly point in the same direction.

chunks.title: The chapter treats persistence as essential to moral reform
chunks.text: Moral improvement cannot depend on temporary enthusiasm. The person must continue the struggle when the initial emotional motivation disappears.

chunks.title: Repeated practice turns difficult obedience into character
chunks.text: A virtue becomes stable when the person repeatedly chooses it. Jihad with the self therefore has a training dimension analogous to building strength through exercise.

chunks.title: Failure should trigger return rather than surrender
chunks.text: A person who falls should not convert one failure into an identity or a reason to abandon the struggle. The important movement is to recognize the failure, correct it and continue.

connections.label: Patience is one of the concrete disciplines by which the self is mastered
Willpower and perseverance depend on the same inner training
The teacher's moral influence requires patience in practice

chunks.title: Patience is an active form of strength
chunks.text: Mazaheri treats sabr as endurance with direction, not passive resignation. It allows a person to remain steady under hardship rather than allowing pain to dictate speech and action.

chunks.title: Patience and gratitude form complementary foundations of faith
chunks.text: The chapter presents patience in hardship alongside gratitude in blessing. Together they keep the believer from being controlled by changing external circumstances.

chunks.title: Patience protects family and professional relationships
chunks.text: The discussion applies sabr to marriage, parenting and teaching: where complete agreement is impossible, patience, forgiveness and perseverance prevent ordinary differences from becoming destructive conflict.

chunks.title: Patience strengthens will and reduces impulsive reaction
chunks.text: The chapter connects endurance with stronger resolve. A person who immediately complains or panics gives temporary circumstances control over his inner state; patience preserves agency.

chunks.title: Trust in God does not eliminate human responsibility
chunks.text: The examples of Moses and the recurring prayer for an expanded chest are used to combine reliance on God with preparation, courage and endurance. The person creates the conditions for action while asking God for the outcome.

chunks.title: Patience is presented as part of faith itself
chunks.text: The chapter uses the image of patience as a structural component of faith, emphasizing that faith without endurance cannot remain stable when circumstances become difficult.

chunks.title: The teacher especially needs patience
chunks.text: Because teaching involves repeated difficulty, imperfect students and emotionally demanding situations, sabr is presented as a practical protection against losing influence through anger, discouragement or harshness.

chunks.title: A patient person can turn hardship into spiritual development
chunks.text: Hardship itself is not automatically beneficial; its value depends on how the person responds. Patience allows difficulty to become an occasion for strengthening character rather than merely a source of resentment.

units.title: گفتار هفتم : ملكه صبر
quotes: يا بني اصبر على الحق و ان كان مراً

connections.label: Self-mastery becomes durable when restraint is trained into a stable disposition
Patience in hardship is developed into a lasting virtue
Teachers need practiced patience to protect their educational influence

chunks.title: A virtue becomes a character-trait through repeated action
chunks.text: Mazaheri distinguishes merely knowing that patience is good from possessing patience as a stable inner disposition. Repeatedly choosing restraint gradually makes the response automatic.

chunks.title: Patience has three forms with increasing moral difficulty
chunks.text: The chapter distinguishes patience in hardship, patience in worship, and patience in avoiding sin. The last is presented as especially difficult because the temptation is attractive rather than merely painful.

chunks.title: Patience in teaching requires deliberate practice
chunks.text: Teachers face immature, provocative and inexperienced students. The practical recommendation is to train patience in these ordinary encounters because repeated reactions shape character.

chunks.title: Tahaqquq through tahallum: acting patiently before patience feels natural
chunks.text: The chapter's practical method is to begin by restraining anger and practicing forbearance even before the inner disposition is fully formed. Action gradually creates the disposition.

chunks.title: Patience in worship turns obligation into stable practice
chunks.text: The goal is not occasional religious enthusiasm but a condition in which obedience becomes natural and increasingly enjoyable. The chapter links this stability to spiritual elevation.

chunks.title: Patience in avoiding sin is a decisive form of self-mastery
chunks.text: The difficult moment is often the moment when desire is available but must be refused. Training oneself to tolerate that deprivation strengthens mastery over the animal dimension.

chunks.title: The chapter connects steadfastness with divine assistance
chunks.text: Qur'anic passages about those who say 'our Lord is God' and then remain steadfast are used to present perseverance as a condition for receiving reassurance and support.

chunks.title: Justice itself is described as a stable moral disposition
chunks.text: The discussion of religious authority and testimony uses the concept of malakah: basic correctness is not enough; reliable moral conduct must become a stable trait.

connections.label: Repeated actions form either virtue or vice
Recognizing the dominant vice prepares the ground for repentance and reform

chunks.title: Jihad with the self includes identifying the forces that defeat judgment
chunks.text: The chapter continues the practical analysis by examining how desire, anger and inner tendencies can distort a person's ability to choose well.

chunks.title: A desire becomes dangerous when it takes command of reason
chunks.text: The moral problem is not simply possessing an inclination. The danger begins when the inclination becomes the decision-maker and reason is recruited afterward to justify it.

chunks.title: Self-awareness is required before self-correction
chunks.text: A person cannot fight an inner tendency that he refuses to recognize. The practical direction is to observe motives and reactions before attempting to reform them.

chunks.title: Small repeated compromises can strengthen a vice
chunks.text: Like virtues, bad traits are built by repeated action. What begins as an occasional compromise can become a stable disposition that later feels normal.

chunks.title: The struggle is both moral and psychological
chunks.text: Mazaheri repeatedly treats the inner battle as something visible in habits, reactions and choices. Spiritual reform therefore requires concrete behavioral discipline rather than abstract intention.

units.title: گفتار نهم :
quotes: إنما التوبة على الله للذين يعملون السوء بجهالة ثم يتوبون من قريب
يا عبادي الذين أسرفوا على أنفسهم لا تقنطوا من رحمة الله

connections.label: Stable virtue requires reversing repeated bad habits through immediate correction
Repentance redirects the same human agency involved in self-mastery
Moral reform requires recognizing and confronting specific vices

chunks.title: Repentance is a form of active self-reconstruction
chunks.text: Repentance is not merely verbal regret. It is a return that changes the person's direction and requires recognition of wrongdoing.

chunks.title: Delay makes repentance harder
chunks.text: The chapter warns against تسویف: postponing repentance on the assumption that there will be a later opportunity. Delay allows the sin to become forgotten, normalized or rationalized.

chunks.title: Rationalization can become a barrier to repentance
chunks.text: When a person builds an explanation that makes his wrongdoing seem justified, he loses the psychological condition necessary for sincere return.

chunks.title: There is no spiritual dead end for the sincere returner
chunks.text: Stories such as Bishr al-Hafi and Hur ibn Yazid are used to emphasize the breadth of divine mercy: even serious wrongdoing does not make sincere repentance impossible.

chunks.title: Shame before God can coexist with forgiveness
chunks.text: Hur's story illustrates an important distinction: forgiveness removes the barrier of guilt, but sincere remorse can remain as a moral memory that prevents returning to the same behavior.

chunks.title: Repentance should be followed by restitution and correction
chunks.text: The chapter does not reduce repentance to feeling bad. The person should repair neglected duties and correct the practical consequences of wrongdoing where possible.

chunks.title: Awareness of God's presence supports moral restraint
chunks.text: Seeing oneself as continually in God's presence is presented as a practical safeguard against hidden wrongdoing and as a source of genuine remorse after failure.

units.title: گفتار دهم :
quotes: آخر ما يخرج عن قلوب الصديقين حب الجاه

connections.label: Vice can block repentance; early recognition therefore matters
The next stage applies self-jihad to specific inner vices
Status-seeking directly conflicts with sincerity

chunks.title: A vice can distort the person's interpretation of his own wrongdoing
chunks.text: The chapter emphasizes that moral danger grows when a person not only sins but becomes unable to see himself as wrong. The inner faculty of self-criticism is then weakened.

chunks.title: Envy can make another person's good feel like one's own loss
chunks.text: The discussion treats envy as a destructive inner condition because it changes the person's relationship with another person's success and can motivate unjust behavior.

chunks.title: Love of status can become an engine of wrongdoing
chunks.text: Ambition for position is presented as especially persistent. A person may knowingly sacrifice truth and justice when recognition or power becomes the overriding goal.

chunks.title: Greed and suspicion can compound one another
chunks.text: When avarice and سوء ظن reinforce each other, the person begins interpreting others through self-interest and becomes increasingly willing to justify unfair behavior.

chunks.title: Vice can prevent repentance by producing self-justification
chunks.text: If a person interprets every wrongdoing as justified, he no longer experiences himself as a sinner who needs to return. The vice therefore becomes a barrier to the remedy itself.

chunks.title: Reform requires early intervention
chunks.text: The chapter's warning is strongest around the beginning of a vice: once it has been repeated and rationalized for years, the person may lose the ability to recognize its seriousness.

chunks.title: Islamic repentance remains open even after serious failure
chunks.text: The warning about hardening the heart is not a doctrine of despair. The chapter pairs the danger of persistent vice with the continuing invitation to return before the habit becomes entrenched.

units.title: گفتار يازدهم : توبه ( 3 )
quotes: انما التوبة على الله للذين يعملون السوء بجهالة ثم يتوبون من قريب
التائب من الذنب كمن لا ذنب له

connections.label: This chapter deepens the earlier warning against delaying repentance
Persistent vices can prevent a person from recognizing the need to repent
Sincere action requires repairing harm rather than merely expressing regret

chunks.title: Repentance is meant to happen before moral numbness sets in
chunks.text: The chapter revisits Qur'an 4:17–18 as a warning: postponing repentance allows repeated sin to make wrongdoing feel ordinary and can weaken the person's ability to recognize his need for return.

chunks.title: The barrier is often loss of moral awareness, not lack of divine mercy
chunks.text: Mazaheri distinguishes between God's willingness to forgive and a sinner's capacity to make a sincere return. A person who no longer regards the act as wrong may not generate genuine repentance.

chunks.title: Sincere repentance is remorse before God, not merely fear of punishment
chunks.text: The discussion of final-moment regret emphasizes that being afraid of hell is not identical to regretting disobedience itself. Genuine tawbah is a moral and relational return.

chunks.title: Rights owed to God require both remorse and practical repair
chunks.text: For neglected obligations such as prayer and fasting, repentance includes making up what was missed rather than treating regret alone as sufficient.

chunks.title: Rights owed to people are especially demanding
chunks.text: The chapter gives حق الناس special weight: repentance requires addressing the human harm or property right involved, not merely asking God privately for forgiveness.

chunks.title: Islamic repentance has no dead end when the return is sincere
chunks.text: The repeated examples of serious sinners who changed direction are used to reinforce the book's central claim that the door of return remains open while genuine repentance is possible.

chunks.title: The best time for repentance is immediately after the wrong
chunks.text: Immediate correction prevents the sin from becoming a repeated pattern and preserves the person's sensitivity to wrongdoing.

connections.label: Immediate correction is the practical antidote to moral drift
Intention is central to sincere action

chunks.title: The chapter applies self-jihad to ordinary moral choices
chunks.text: The struggle with the self is shown in everyday decisions rather than only extraordinary spiritual states.

chunks.title: Intention changes the moral meaning of an outward action
chunks.text: A person's inner motive can transform an apparently good action into self-serving behavior, making examination of intention part of practical self-discipline.

chunks.title: Repeated choices gradually reveal the dominant direction of the self
chunks.text: The chapter treats habits as evidence of what a person has allowed to become stronger inside him. Self-knowledge therefore comes from watching repeated choices.

chunks.title: The remedy is deliberate correction before the habit hardens
chunks.text: Once a person notices a recurring tendency, he should intervene through contrary practice instead of waiting for the problem to disappear by itself.

connections.label: The malakah of patience is the clearest example of repeated practice
Vices also become stable dispositions through repetition

chunks.title: Moral character is built through repeated conduct
chunks.text: The chapter continues the malakah framework: actions are not isolated events but exercises that strengthen a disposition.

chunks.title: The same mechanism can create virtue or vice
chunks.text: Repeated patience can become patience as a stable quality, while repeated anger, harshness or selfishness can become equally stable vices.

chunks.title: Self-jihad therefore requires behavioral practice
chunks.text: Knowing a virtue intellectually is insufficient. The person must deliberately create situations in which the desired response is practiced until it becomes easier and more natural.

chunks.title: A stable disposition eventually changes what feels pleasurable
chunks.text: The mature stage of moral training is not merely forcing oneself to do the right thing; the right action gradually becomes the action the person wants.

connections.label: Teachers influence students through conduct, including speech
Controlling speech requires the same repeated practice that creates patience
Fulfilling one's duty includes protecting others from avoidable harm

chunks.title: Speech is a major arena of jihad with the self
chunks.text: The chapter turns strongly toward the moral consequences of speech: words can build relationships and education, but careless speech can create lasting damage.

chunks.title: A true statement can still be unwise to say
chunks.text: Mazaheri distinguishes truthfulness from indiscriminate speaking. A statement may be factually true yet needlessly harmful, inflammatory or inappropriate to the setting.

chunks.title: Unnecessary speech creates consequences beyond the moment
chunks.text: Stories in the chapter illustrate how a casual joke, insult or unnecessary claim can produce resentment, humiliation, conflict and even serious retaliation.

chunks.title: The tongue can manufacture a person's social identity
chunks.text: Repeated mockery, sarcasm, backbiting, accusation or excessive talk can become a recognizable character trait. What begins as speech becomes a disposition and eventually shapes how others experience the person.

chunks.title: Words can damage family relationships irreversibly
chunks.text: The chapter emphasizes that a wound caused by a sharp remark can be difficult to repair. Repeated verbal injury can accumulate until affection is replaced by resentment and family life collapses.

chunks.title: People with influence have a higher obligation to control speech
chunks.text: Teachers, respected figures and public-facing people can magnify the effects of careless words. Mazaheri therefore calls for thinking before speaking and exercising particular restraint at home.

chunks.title: The practical rule is simple: think before speaking
chunks.text: The chapter's broad discipline is to ask whether a statement has a useful worldly or spiritual purpose before saying it. Silence is often safer than speech that merely satisfies impulse.

quotes.text: بدان كه تو عبدى و او مولاست
العبد و ما في يده كان لمولاه

connections.label: The inner struggle becomes concrete submission to God rather than merely resisting desire
Patience and steadiness depend on the believer's response to hardship and ease
Expanded inner capacity makes obedience and self-control sustainable
Servitude is the foundation from which sincerity and God-directed action become possible

chunks.title: Respect for the Qur'an is itself part of spiritual discipline
chunks.text: The discourse begins by insisting that the Qur'an must be heard with silence, attention and respect. Mazaheri treats the manner in which a person approaches revelation as morally significant, not as a merely ceremonial detail.

chunks.title: The Qur'an is presented as a refuge when life becomes confusing or dark
chunks.text: The prophetic narration cited in the chapter presents the Qur'an as a guide and refuge during fitnah. Making the Qur'an one's guide is therefore described as something that shapes the direction of one's life, not merely something consulted for information.

chunks.title: The inner battle is the central arena of jihad
chunks.text: Mazaheri describes the conflict between the human/spiritual dimension and the animal/desiring dimension as a permanent inner war, calling victory in this arena jihad al-akbar. Losing this struggle means allowing the lower side of the person to govern the whole self.

chunks.title: The goal of inner victory is the tranquil soul
chunks.text: The chapter contrasts collapse in the inner struggle with the Qur'anic image of al-nafs al-mutma'innah. The mature endpoint is not simply avoiding sins but reaching a state of tranquility in which the person is accepted by God and willingly returns to Him.

chunks.title: Servitude begins with recognizing the Creator-servant relationship
chunks.text: In the counsel attributed to Imam al-Sadiq, the first condition for expanded spiritual capacity is recognizing that one is a servant and God is the Master. Mazaheri presents genuine servitude as radical orientation toward God's will rather than treating oneself as autonomous.

chunks.title: Submission to God is compatible with confidence in His justice and mercy
chunks.text: The slave-and-master story is explicitly qualified: unconditional obedience is appropriate to God because God is just and merciful, not because human masters may legitimately abuse servants. Trust in divine wisdom changes how a believer interprets both hardship and blessing.

chunks.title: The believer should be stable in hardship and prosperity
chunks.text: Mazaheri contrasts the unstable person who is carried away by either calamity or prosperity with the believer described as firm like a mountain. Servitude means receiving both difficulty and ease within the larger frame of submission to God.

chunks.title: Obedience is a practical expression of servitude
chunks.text: The second counsel to Sufyan al-Thawri connects servitude to pursuing God's pleasure, taking obligations seriously and avoiding what brings divine displeasure. Jihad with the self is therefore translated into concrete daily obedience rather than vague spiritual feeling.

chunks.title: Everything a person possesses is entrusted by God and should be used accordingly
chunks.text: The third counsel states that the servant and whatever is in his possession belong to the Master. Mazaheri applies this to money, health, intellect, safety and knowledge: recognizing them as divine gifts makes using them for God's purposes and for other people a natural consequence of servitude.

units.title: گفتار شانزدهم : فعاليت ، استقامت و توبه به جوانب كار

quotes.text: فعاليت ، استقامت و توجه به جوانب كار
بحث اخلاقى گفتن و شنيدنش آسان است ، اما عمل كردن به بحث اخلاقى دشوار است

connections.label: Patience becomes perseverance when it is translated into sustained action
Repeated effort turns a virtue from an idea into a stable disposition
Repentance is presented as an active force that interrupts moral decline
Servitude requires disciplined use of one's abilities rather than passivity
Sustained work needs a God-directed motive so effort does not become ego-driven ambition

chunks.title: Faith, patience, repentance and expanded capacity are supports for defeating the self
chunks.text: The chapter gathers earlier lessons into a practical system: deepened faith through serious worship, patience in difficulty and obedience, repentance as an inner upheaval, and sadr expansion as capacities that strengthen a person in the inner struggle.

chunks.title: Victory requires activity, perseverance and attention to the whole task
chunks.text: Mazaheri identifies three practical requirements for success: activity, perseverance and attention to the different sides of a task. Talent alone is not treated as decisive; sustained effort and careful attention can compensate for limited natural ability.

chunks.title: The example of Maytham al-Tammar illustrates rapid growth through disciplined effort
chunks.text: Maytham is presented as an example of someone whose sustained activity, perseverance and attention transformed his capacities. His closeness to Imam Ali and his later courage are used to show what disciplined spiritual development can produce.

chunks.title: Extraordinary spiritual abilities are not the real measure of human success
chunks.text: The chapter uses stories of people with unusual abilities to make a larger distinction: feats such as extraordinary physical or spiritual capacities are not the highest achievement. Becoming genuinely human by mastering the commanding self is the more important victory.

chunks.title: The same principle applies to worldly and spiritual work
chunks.text: Mazaheri argues that a believer should actively pursue both worldly responsibilities and the afterlife. The Qur'anic balance is not withdrawal from productive life but using one's God-given intellect, health, youth, security and wealth for both domains.

chunks.title: Moral decline accelerates when the person stops guarding the inner struggle
chunks.text: The chapter describes decline as progressive: neglect begins with losing the sweetness of worship, then can reach denial of religious truth, pleasure in sin and eventually pleasure in ظلم and cruelty. The warning is that the self does not have a natural stopping point once disciplined resistance is abandoned.

chunks.title: Repeated wrongdoing can make serious sin feel ordinary
chunks.text: Mazaheri uses backbiting, slander and attacking people's dignity to illustrate a lower-level form of moral collapse. A person may remain sensitive to physical violence while becoming insensitive to harming reputations, showing that habituation can normalize grave wrongdoing.

chunks.title: The practical conclusion is to keep working against the self rather than assuming safety
chunks.text: The chapter closes by treating jihad with the self as an ongoing activity. Without activity, perseverance and attention, the person moves toward decline; with them, even a difficult starting point can become a path of ascent.

quotes.text: اگر با خدا باشيد خدا با شماست
انما نطعمكم لوجه الله نريد منكم جزاء و لاشكورا
صبغه الله و من احسن من الله صبغه

connections.label: Servitude becomes sincere when the person's real motive is God rather than the self
Activity and perseverance need a purified motive to become spiritual progress rather than egoic ambition
Night prayer is presented as one practical means of building a God-centered inner life
The teacher's influence becomes trustworthy when teaching is done for God rather than recognition

chunks.title: Sincerity means giving one's thoughts, speech and actions a God-directed orientation
chunks.text: Mazaheri defines the practical direction of ikhlas broadly: not only outward actions but thoughts, speech, intentions and motives should be oriented toward God. This turns sincerity into a governing orientation of life rather than a property of a few religious acts.

chunks.title: God-centered action is presented as the source of divine assistance
chunks.text: The chapter links sincere orientation to the promise that God supports those who support His cause. In the context of jihad with the self, reliance on divine help is presented as necessary because the person cannot reliably defeat the lower self through isolated willpower.

chunks.title: Taking desire, ego or worldly recognition as the ultimate motive is a form of misplaced worship
chunks.text: Mazaheri argues that when desire, Satan or worldly interests become the controlling motive of thought and action, the person has effectively made them an object of worship. Ikhlas therefore requires examining what actually moves a person, not merely what the action looks like externally.

chunks.title: Sincerity changes ordinary family work into worship
chunks.text: The chapter applies ikhlas to domestic life: caring for children, serving a spouse and enduring household work can become worship when performed for God rather than for praise, repayment or recognition. The same outward action can therefore have a radically different spiritual meaning depending on its motive.

chunks.title: Expecting recognition creates resentment when recognition fails
chunks.text: Mazaheri repeatedly contrasts God-directed action with the expectation of thanks. When a person works for praise, unmet expectations generate anger, jealousy, hurt and conflict; when God is the motive, the absence of human recognition does not invalidate the work.

chunks.title: Sincerity can turn difficult service into something spiritually bearable
chunks.text: The chapter applies the same logic to earning for one's family and teaching students. If the purpose is God and the fulfillment of responsibility, ordinary frustrations such as status, salary comparison or lack of appreciation lose their power to determine one's emotional state.

chunks.title: The standard of sincere giving is to seek no repayment or praise
chunks.text: The example of the governor of Homs and the Qur'anic phrase 'for the face of God' illustrate the mature form of giving: even when a person is criticized by the people he serves, he can respond with further good because the act was not purchased by their praise.

chunks.title: Divine coloration is presented as a durable identity rather than a temporary performance
chunks.text: Mazaheri uses the Qur'anic image of God's color to distinguish lasting spiritual formation from a temporary outward appearance. When God's orientation becomes the motive of thought, intention and action, the person gradually becomes harder for Satan and the commanding self to manipulate.

connections.label: Night prayer is presented as practical training in servitude and submission
Consistent night worship requires gradual activity and perseverance rather than a burst of effort
Hidden worship provides a concrete arena for sincerity because it is less dependent on public recognition
Gradual practice is what turns a difficult discipline into a stable habit

chunks.title: Night prayer is presented as a practical instrument for inner victory
chunks.text: The chapter argues that late-night worship is not an ornamental extra: it strengthens the person in the struggle against the commanding self, brings vitality and helps loosen the grip of worldly anxiety.

chunks.title: The recommended practice is gradual rather than self-destructive
chunks.text: Mazaheri explicitly warns against exhausting the self through an extreme initial schedule. He recommends starting with a manageable period before dawn and gradually extending wakefulness as the discipline becomes sustainable.

chunks.title: The Qur'an's language about night worship supports flexibility in how much one performs
chunks.text: The discussion of al-Muzzammil is used to emphasize that night worship can be practiced according to one's capacity. The point is persistent participation, not an all-or-nothing standard that causes a person to abandon the practice.

chunks.title: Prayer at its proper time, especially morning prayer, is tied to the discipline of night worship
chunks.text: The chapter connects night prayer with maintaining the obligatory morning prayer and emphasizes the special importance assigned to Fajr. Night worship is therefore framed within a larger rhythm of timely obligatory worship rather than as a substitute for it.

chunks.title: Knowing the value of a practice is easier than actually performing it
chunks.text: Mazaheri distinguishes intellectual agreement from moral action: people may readily understand that night worship is valuable while still failing to rise when the alarm rings. This illustrates the broader framework of jihad with the self—knowledge must become repeated behavior.

chunks.title: Daytime conduct can affect whether a person succeeds in rising at night
chunks.text: The chapter links daytime sins and unlawful or careless conduct with difficulty waking for night prayer. The broader lesson is that spiritual practices are interconnected: what a person does during the day can either strengthen or weaken the next act of worship.

chunks.title: Night worship is described as having consequences beyond the private moment
chunks.text: The chapter presents the possibility that consistent worship changes the person's standing in the unseen world, including divine and angelic assistance. Whether understood as spiritual formation or as the chapter's narration of unseen effects, the teaching is that hidden discipline has consequences larger than the immediate act.

chunks.title: Spiritual discipline must remain balanced and guided
chunks.text: Mazaheri warns that self-improvement can itself become excessive if pursued without balance or guidance. The proper path combines worship with moderation, and he recommends learning ethical practice under knowledgeable guidance rather than turning a good discipline into harmful extremism.

chunks.title: The chapter's final method is to train the self patiently until worship becomes sustainable
chunks.text: The closing advice returns to gradual training: regulate sleep, begin with a manageable amount, keep the obligatory prayers central, and increase practice over time. The same 'bridle the difficult horse without exhausting it' principle from earlier discussions is applied directly to night worship.
